bib.title: It’s Not Just Size That Matters: Small Language Models Are Also Few-Shot Learners

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "It's Not Just Size That Matters: Small Language Models Are Also Few-Shot Learners", Timo Schick and Hinrich Schütze (LMU Munich / Sulzer GmbH). NAACL-HLT 2021, pages 2339–2352 (arXiv 2009.07118). PDF: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/01-prompt-engineering/sources/schick-2021-its-not-just-size-that.pdf

COVERAGE: All 60,076 chars. I read characters 0–40,000 in full. That covers the body, Tables 1–6, the conclusion and the start of the references. I read 50,000–60,076 in full, which covers the end of the references, Appendix A (training details, Table 7 hyperparameters) and Appendix B (dataset details, Table 8). For 40,000–50,000, which is references only, I searched for the origin entries (PET 2021, ALBERT) and did not read every line. Nothing that holds results was skipped.

CLAIMS
- claim: ALBERT trained with PET/iPET on 32 labelled examples does slightly better than 175B GPT-3 primed with 32 in-context examples on SuperGLUE, with about 0.1% of the parameters.
  number: test average PET 74.0, iPET 75.4, GPT-3 71.8. Parameters 223M vs 175,000M.
  setup: The model is ALBERT-xxlarge-v2 (223M). Training uses the FewGLUE set of 32 labelled examples per task plus up to 20,000 unlabelled examples per task. It is fine-tuned with gradients, with no dev-set hyperparameter tuning. GPT-3's numbers are the ones Brown et al. reported for priming with 32 examples and no gradient updates. The labelled examples are not the same ones GPT-3 used.
  quote: "PET 223 79.1 87.2 / 60.2 90.8 67.2 50.7 88.4 36.4 / 76.6 85.4 / 85.9 74.0" / "iPET 223 81.2 88.8 / 79.9 90.8 70.8 49.3 88.4 31.7 / 74.1 85.4 / 85.9 75.4" / "GPT-3 175,000 76.4 75.6 / 52.0 92.0 69.0 49.4 80.1 30.5 / 75.4 90.2 / 91.1 71.8"; "PET and its iterative variant (iPET) both outperform GPT-3 on SuperGLUE with 32 training examples, while requiring only 0.1% of its parameters"
  where: Table 1, p.2344 (offset about 27–28k); Intro p.2340
- claim: At a similar size, PET beats primed GPT-3 by 18 points. GPT-3 175B is 785 times larger than ALBERT.
  number: 18 points vs GPT-3 Med (350M); factor 785
  setup: SuperGLUE dev averages. PET 74.1, GPT-3 Med 56.2, GPT-3 175B 73.2.
  quote: "ALBERT with PET performs similar to the largest GPT-3 model, which is larger by a factor of 785. On average, PET performs 18 points better compared to GPT-3 Med, a model of similar size."
  where: p.2344–2345
- claim: In primed GPT-3, few-shot gains grow with model size. Small GPT-3 models barely beat chance, and 32 examples help little over one example. For small models, more examples can make results worse.
  number: dev averages are Small 50.1, Med 56.2, Large 56.8, XL 60.0, 2.7B 64.3, 6.7B 63.6, 13B 66.9, 175B 73.2
  setup: Figure 5 compares GPT-3 primed with 32 examples against one-shot. The authors avoid a zero-shot baseline because zero-shot GPT-3 is below chance on some tasks.
  quote: "priming with 32 examples only slightly improves performance for most tasks and model sizes. For some tasks, adding more examples even leads to worse performance, especially for smaller models. For ReCoRD, even the largest model's performance slightly drops when adding more examples." Footnote: "zero-shot GPT-3 performs well below random guessing for some tasks (e.g., 0.0% accuracy for WiC)"
  where: Sec 5.3, p.2347; Table 1 dev rows p.2344
  NOTE FOR 03-core-techniques: The paper supports "in-context few-shot emerges with scale". It does not support the broader idea that small models cannot learn from a few examples. Its own point is that small models can when the examples go into gradient updates.
- claim: When the same small model does in-context priming instead of PET, PET wins by a wide margin.
  number: CB 88.7/83.0 vs 56.3/37.7; RTE 60.4 vs 49.5
  setup: XLNet, because ALBERT's 512-token limit cannot fit 32 examples. On MultiRC, priming was infeasible because the examples need more than 10,000 tokens.
  quote: "PET (XLNet) 88.7 / 83.0 60.4 21.4 / 66.6 63.4" / "Priming (XLNet) 56.3 / 37.7 49.5 – / – –"; "the 32 examples in FewGLUE would require more than 10,000 tokens"
  where: Table 3, Sec 5.3, p.2346
- claim: PET beats both plain supervised fine-tuning without patterns and zero-shot pattern use on the same 32 examples.
  number: average 66.6 PET vs 43.0 supervised vs 38.5 unsupervised (CB/RTE/MultiRC)
  setup: ALBERT, FewGLUE
  quote: "PET 85.1 / 59.4 69.8 37.9 / 77.3 66.6" / "unsupervised 33.5 / 23.1 55.0 3.9 / 60.3 38.5" / "supervised 60.7 / 42.5 50.2 4.3 / 49.8 43.0"
  where: Table 3, p.2346
- claim: You do not need unlabelled data to get the performance. An ensemble without distillation does as well or better. Unlabelled data only serves to distil the ensemble into one small model.
  number: average 68.0 (no distillation) vs 66.6 (distilled) for p_ours; 70.4 vs 68.3 for p_comb
  setup: ALBERT, CB/RTE/MultiRC. The ensemble is 3·k models for k PVPs.
  quote: "if the goal is only to achieve good performance, then unlabeled data is not necessary; however, it is required to obtain a single, lightweight model as ﬁnal classiﬁer." / "the ensemble for k PVPs is larger than the distilled model by a factor of 3· k ... even for a large number of PVPs the ensemble is smaller than GPT-3 by two orders of magnitude."
  where: Sec 5.2, Table 2, p.2345–2346
- claim: How a task is worded as a prompt (pattern) shifts results by many points. Combining several patterns makes up for weak ones.
  number: MultiRC EM 37.9 (p_ours) vs 25.4 (p_GPT-3); RTE 69.8 vs 71.8; combined average 68.3 vs 66.6 / 63.1
  quote: "PET (pours) 85.1 / 59.4 69.8 37.9 / 77.3 66.6" / "PET (pGPT-3) 83.3 / 58.1 71.8 25.4 / 68.3 63.1" / "PET (pcomb) 84.5 / 59.0 74.7 39.1 / 77.7 68.3"
  where: Table 2, Sec 5.1, p.2345
- claim: The choice of base LM matters. Bidirectional ALBERT is far better than RoBERTa and unidirectional GPT-2 at a similar size.
  number: averages 71.8 ALBERT (223M), 63.7 RoBERTa (355M), 52.0 GPT-2 (345M)
  setup: PET without distillation. p_GPT-3 for CB/RTE, p_ours for MultiRC.
  quote: "exchanging ALBERT with RoBERTa results in an average performance drop of 8 points. However, RoBERTa still clearly outperforms GPT-3 13B, which is larger by two orders of magnitude."
  where: Table 4, Sec 5.4, p.2347
- claim: Which 32 examples are chosen shifts PET's results a lot, more than it shifts GPT-3's. The average stays close to GPT-3 across seeds.
  number: averages 68.0 / 63.2 / 67.6 across three seeds vs GPT-3 65.4; RTE 66.4 vs 61.4
  quote: "GPT-3 82.1 / 57.2 72.9 32.5 / 74.8 65.4" / "PET¬dist (Σ1) 82.1 / 57.4 61.4 39.2 / 77.9 63.2"; "changing the set of training examples can result in large performance differences for PET"
  where: Table 6, Sec 5.6, p.2348
- claim: The approach is cheap. It runs on a single 11GB GPU in hours, without hyperparameter search.
  number: 250 steps in about 45 minutes; final classifier 5,000 steps in 2.5 hours
  quote: "training a single PET model for 250 steps took approximately 45 minutes. Depending on the task, labeling unlabeled examples took 0.2–1.5 hours per model. Training the ﬁnal classiﬁer for 5,000 steps on the soft-labeled dataset took 2.5 hours on average."
  where: Appendix A, p.2351
- claim: Both methods are still far below full-data fine-tuning.
  number: SotA test average 89.3 (T5, 11,000M)
  quote: "SotA 11,000 91.2 93.9 / 96.8 94.8 92.5 76.9 93.8 88.1 / 63.3 94.1 / 93.4 89.3"; "it still clearly performs worse than a state-of-the-art model trained on the regular, full size SuperGLUE training set."
  where: Table 1 and p.2345
- claim: Priming does not scale past a few examples because of the context window.
  number: 2,048 tokens (GPT-3)
  quote: "It does not scale to more than a few examples as the context window of most LMs is limited to a few hundred tokens." / "While GPT-3 can process up to 2,048 tokens, this is still not enough to ﬁt≥32 examples for some SuperGLUE tasks."
  where: Intro p.2339 and fn 2

WHAT THE HEAD-TO-HEAD HOLDS EQUAL AND WHAT IT DOES NOT
- Equal: the count of 32 labelled examples per task. For MultiRC and ReCoRD, "select a total of 32 questions – which corresponds to more than 32 training examples – to enable a fair comparison with GPT-3" (App B). Both use the SuperGLUE test set.
- Not equal: (1) the specific examples. GPT-3 "uses a different set of training examples for each test example", and the authors could not obtain those sets (Sec 4). (2) Learning mode. PET updates weights; GPT-3 does in-context learning only. (3) Unlabelled data. PET's distilled numbers use up to 20,000 unlabelled examples per task. For RTE and CB these are padded with MNLI examples, which is extra in-domain text GPT-3 never sees. iPET also self-labels this data. (4) Patterns. PET combines several hand-designed PVPs, while GPT-3 used one prompt. (5) Architecture. PET uses a bidirectional MLM, GPT-3 a unidirectional one. (6) iPET was not run on COPA, WSC or ReCoRD, so their PET numbers were reused. The GPT-3 numbers come from Brown et al. The authors could not run GPT-3 themselves ("We could not obtain access to OpenAI's GPT-3 API").

LIMITS
- Classification and multiple-choice NLU in English only (SuperGLUE). Generative tasks are left to future work.
- Hand-written patterns and verbalizers are needed for each task. The original PET only handled single-token verbalizers, and multi-token support is this paper's addition.
- The authors concede that unlabelled data "may not always be the case in real-world settings."
- High variance across training sets (Table 6).
- Cross-model comparisons (Fig. 5, bottom row) are "not directly comparable due to different underlying models and PVPs."
- The GPT-2 shortfall may be due to pretraining data rather than unidirectionality (the authors say so).
- Dated: the GPT-3 baseline is the 2020 base model before instruction tuning. The comparison predates instruction-tuned LLMs, long context windows and parameter-efficient fine-tuning, so the 2,048-token argument is obsolete.

BUILDS ON
- PET/iPET: Schick and Schütze (2021), "Exploiting cloze questions for few shot text classification and natural language inference", EACL.
- Knowledge distillation: Hinton et al., 2015.
- Self-training: Scudder, 1965; Yarowsky, 1995; Brin, 1999; McClosky et al., 2006.
- Zero-shot with task descriptions: Radford et al. (2019).
- Priming / in-context learning baseline: Brown et al. (2020).
- MLM as sequence scorer: Wang and Cho, 2019; Salazar et al. (2020); Ghazvininejad et al. (2019).
- Base model: ALBERT, Lan et al. (2020).
- Multi-class hinge loss: Weston and Watkins, 1999; Dogan et al., 2016.
- Green AI framing: Schwartz et al., 2020a; Strubell et al., 2019.

CODE
- Repo: "https://github.com/timoschick/pet" (fn 1, p.2339). Dataset: "https://github.com/timoschick/fewglue" (fn 5, p.2342).
- Example pattern-verbalizer pair (BoolQ), verbatim: "p. Question: q? Answer: __." with yes/true vs no/false verbalizers (p.2342). This is a compact illustration of a "prompt as cloze template".
- Hyperparameters (Table 7, p.2352): "learning_rate 1e-5", "pet_max_steps 250", "sc_max_steps 5,000", "max_seq_length 256".

FIGURES
- Figure 1 (p.1/2339): "Performance on SuperGLUE with 32 training examples. ALBERT with PET/iPET outperforms GPT-3 although it is much 'greener' in that it has three orders of magnitude fewer parameters." This is a log-parameter vs score plot. In one image it shows GPT-3's few-shot score rising with scale and the small PET point sitting above it. It is the best candidate for the "emerges with scale, unless you fine-tune" point.
- Figure 5 (p.8/2346): "Accuracy differences between priming with 32 examples and one-shot priming for all GPT-3 models as well as between ALBERT with PET (without distillation) and unsupervised ALBERT (bottom row)". This heatmap shows that adding in-context examples helps little, or hurts in small models, while PET's gains are large. It fits 03-core-techniques.
- Figure 2 (p.2/2340): a PVP converting an RTE pair into the cloze "Oil prices rise ? __ , Oil prices fall back ." with Yes/No verbalizers. It shows prompt-as-template plus verbalizer faster than prose does, which fits 04-controlling-output (fine-tuning with prompts).
- Figure 4 (p.7): the iPET generations figure. It is less useful for these notes.
- Figure 3: multi-token decoding. Too technical for these notes.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction is clean. Ligatures (ﬁ) and some math symbols are garbled in equations (Eqs. 1–5). Figure 1 and 5 axis labels came through as loose text.
- Table cells are space-separated, but the column order matches the header "BoolQ CB COPA RTE WiC WSC MultiRC ReCoRD Avg".
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
- I did not read every line of the 40k–50k reference block, as noted under COVERAGE.
